---
title: "Quiz: interpolating, approximating and smoothing splines"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** You have 40 noisy samples of a growth curve. Why is the interpolating spline a poor choice, and what are the two alternatives?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the curve do with the noise?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It passes through every sample, so it reproduces the noise as wiggles (and its derivatives are worse). Alternatives: an **approximating** spline with fewer control points, fitted by least squares; or a **smoothing** spline that keeps one value per sample but penalises bending (data + λ·bending).
:::

---

**Q2.** Among all smooth curves through a set of points, which one bends least? What does "bends least" mean here?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The draftsman's wooden strip.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The natural cubic spline (zero curvature at the two ends). "Bends least" means the smallest bending energy $\int f''(x)^2\,dx$.
:::

---

**Q3.** In a smoothing spline, what do you get for λ = 0 and for λ → ∞?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which curves have zero bending energy?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
λ = 0: no penalty, so the interpolating (natural) spline through every point. λ → ∞: any bending is infinitely expensive, so the curve must be a straight line; among lines, the least-squares line.
:::

---

**Q4.** Three samples $(0, 3, 0)$ are smoothed with the discrete penalty λ·(second difference)². What happens to their mean as λ grows? Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is the second difference of a constant?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The mean stays 1: λ = 1 gives $(0.857, 1.286, 0.857)$, λ → ∞ gives $(1, 1, 1)$. The penalty does not see constants (or lines), so it cannot move the mean; it only removes the bend.
:::

---

**Q5.** Leave-one-out cross-validation gives a U-shaped curve over λ. Explain both arms of the U.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Predict a hidden point with a curve that is too wiggly, and with one that is too stiff.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Small λ: the curve chases the noise of its neighbours, so it predicts a hidden point badly (high variance). Large λ: the curve is too stiff to follow the true shape (high bias). The minimum balances the two.
:::

---

**Q6.** The noise in your data doubles. Should the λ chosen by cross-validation go up or down?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
More noise, more smoothing.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Up: noisier data need more smoothing. In the demo's kink data, the CV choice goes from λ ≈ 0.35 (noise 0.25) to λ ≈ 1.0 (noise 0.5), and the effective number of parameters from 7.2 to 5.8.
:::

---

**Q7.** Why is the perimeter of a segmented disc by edge count 27 % too long, whatever the radius? How does a spline fit avoid this?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Add up the horizontal and the vertical edges of the staircase.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The staircase's horizontal edges add up to twice the width and its vertical edges to twice the height: $4 \cdot 2r = 8r$ instead of $2\pi r$, a ratio $4/\pi = 1.27$. A spline fitted to the boundary is a smooth curve close to the true outline; its length is the integral of its speed (62.9 for a radius-10 disc, true 62.8).
:::

---

**Q8.** Smoothing an outline with Fourier descriptors (few terms) or with a smoothing spline: which one changes the outline far from a sharp corner? Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Global waves versus local bumps.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Fourier descriptors: each term is a wave around the whole outline, so dropping the high frequencies that the corner needs makes ripples everywhere (ringing). The spline's basis functions are local bumps: smoothing rounds the corner and leaves the rest almost unchanged.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Write the normal equations of the penalised least-squares problem $\min_{\mathbf{c}}\|\mathbf{y} - B\mathbf{c}\|^2 + \lambda\mathbf{c}^\top P\mathbf{c}$ ($P$ symmetric).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Set the gradient with respect to $\mathbf{c}$ to zero.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Gradient: $-2B^\top(\mathbf{y} - B\mathbf{c}) + 2\lambda P\mathbf{c} = 0$, so $(B^\top B + \lambda P)\mathbf{c} = B^\top\mathbf{y}$.
:::
